The primitive. Evaluated-and-denied MUST be distinguishable from never-evaluated. A DENY that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from an action nobody looked at, and a consumer cannot tell “the policy refused this” from “the policy never saw it.”
Why it belongs in guidance, not an implementation. Three builds arrived independently: ZK-anchored (your denial circuit), attested, and recompute. None referenced the others. A rule rediscovered three times by people not talking about it is a property of the boundary, not of any codebase.
What a conforming verifier must expose. A DENY produces a positive on-chain trace under the same interface as an ALLOW — isDenied as the mirror of consumption, not a missing record. The absence of a record is never a verdict.
The corollary that bites. Could-not-evaluate is a third state, not a DENY. An unreachable policy engine, an expired verdict, an unregistered domain — none of those are denials, and collapsing them into DENY makes a liveness failure look like a policy decision.
Negative-vector requirement. Conformance means a test for the unevaluated case specifically, not only the denied one. The two are trivially confused and only one of them is checked by default.
Point 4 is the one I’d most want your eye on: I think deny-if-not-allowed (your indexed-tree future work) sits precisely there. Non-membership in an allowlist is not-permitted, which is a different claim from denied — and once both exist they both prove decision = 0, against different roots, byte-identically. Worth deciding whether that distinction lives in policy_root semantics, in a policy_kind public input, or in domain separation, before proofs exist at scale. Your own encoding-freeze comment is why now is cheap and later is not.

The two-tier split is right, and the last message is the important one: try deterministic verification first, fall back to humans. That ordering is the whole game. Five notes, roughly in order of how much they change the design.

1 · The routing decision is currently unadjudicated
“The workflow first checks whether on-chain verification paths are available. It uses those if possible.”

Whoever decides whether a dispute is on-chain verifiable decides which tier rules it, and therefore decides the outcome. That decision is the highest-leverage lever in the system and right now nothing governs it.

Concretely: a colluding majority does not need to win Tier 2, it only needs to reach Tier 2. If routing is automatic on “is a proof available,” then anyone who can make an attestation unavailable — let it expire, withhold it, break a TEE quote’s freshness — has routed the dispute into the capturable tier. Availability becomes the attack surface, and the attack looks like an outage rather than an attack.

Fix: route per-claim, predeclared. The workflow names, before the task starts, which claims are verifiable by which mechanism. A claim declared ZK-verifiable that arrives without a proof is not “unverifiable, escalate” — it is failed. Absence of the promised proof is a verdict against the party who owed it, never a routing change.

This is the same rule as pinning a recompute recipe before the run rather than choosing one after seeing the output.

2 · Verifiability is a property of each claim, not of the dispute
“Few real-world tasks are fully machine-recomputable.” True of tasks. Not true of the claims inside them.

Almost any dispute decomposes:

claim who settles it
the worker actually ran the thing recomputable — attestation / provenance
on the agreed input, unmodified recomputable — input-binding hash (WYRIWE-shaped)
at a time within the window recomputable — anchor
against the agreed policy or spec version recomputable — pinned ref
the output is good subjective — Tier 2
Only the last row is irreducibly social. Today the design sends the whole dispute to Tier 2; it should send the residue, with the mechanical rows already settled and handed over as established fact.

There is a sharper way to say why this matters, which only became obvious writing it up. The funding note argues this group can derive a contribution split rather than vote on it, because the record here is already machine-checkable. Your design votes. Those look like opposing answers and they are not — they are the same answer at different scopes: derive everything that can be derived, and vote only on the remainder. The disagreement is only about how large the remainder is, and the remainder is much smaller than a whole dispute.

That matters because of your own stated risk — Tier 2 is the trust root, collusion inside it breaks everything. The answer to a dangerous trust root is not a better trust root. It is giving it less to decide. A Tier 2 that rules only on “was the quality acceptable,” having been told as fact what ran, on what, when, and against which spec, is enormously harder to capture than one ruling on the whole story.

3 · Agent voting silently breaks the N² claim
Super-linear security scales with N independent participants. The N² collusion cost assumes the N fail independently.

If votes are cast by AI agents, and those agents are the same model with the same prompt over the same evidence, then N agents are one opinion counted N times. The effective N collapses, and the collusion cost collapses with it — while the headline number still says N². Nothing in the system measures this, so the security claim degrades silently.

The mapping “every agent maps back to a human stakeholder” fixes accountability, not correlation. Ten humans running the same model are ten accountable parties producing one judgement.

Fix: independence must be derived and disclosed, not assumed from the participant count. Voters declare model identity and ancestry, prompt/scaffold hash, and evidence source — and the effective N used for the economic bound is computed from distinct configurations, not from headcount. Where they correlate, the bond requirement rises rather than the count.

Worth saying: this is the third context this week where independence turned out to be asserted by labelling rather than derived. It is not a niche failure.

4 · Checkpointing spreads risk and starves challenges
Breaking settlement into many small checkpoints does reduce one-shot capture. But challenger bonds and effort are roughly fixed per challenge, while the value at stake per checkpoint falls with the slicing.

Past a certain granularity, no rational watchdog bonds against a checkpoint worth less than the bond. That is precisely your open risk — if no watchdog steps forward, misbehaviour goes undetected — and checkpointing makes it worse, not better, at the margin.

Fix: challenge economics must scale with the aggregate at risk, not the slice. Either a successful challenge at one checkpoint reopens the prior settled checkpoints in that window, or bonds and rewards are pooled across the window. Otherwise fine-grained settlement is a way to make cheating profitable in small pieces.

5 · The design currently pays people to notice and stay quiet
“Minority dissenters get paid normally unless they raise a challenge.”

So dissent is free, and challenge costs a bond that can be slashed. For an honest worker who has spotted collusion, the dominant strategy is to dissent quietly and take payment. The gap between noticing and acting is entirely unfunded, and it is the same gap as risk 1.

Fix: pay correct dissent, not only successful challenge. A dissenting minority later vindicated should draw from the slashed pool. Noticing should have positive expected value on its own, with the bond buying escalation rather than buying the right to be right.

Where this leaves the shape. Tier 1 unchanged. Tier 2 much smaller, ruling only on the subjective residue. A predeclared per-claim routing table sitting between them, in which a missing promised proof is a loss rather than an escalation. And the economic layer computing its bound from derived independence rather than headcount.

Happy to write up the per-claim routing table as a concrete schema if useful — it is close to something we already have machinery for.

§ Non-suppression and the verdict state space
(draft for the ERC-8274 guidance layer — cut freely)

1 · The primitive
A verifier that can only report a positive result cannot be used to establish absence.

Evaluated-and-denied MUST be distinguishable from never-evaluated. A denial that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from an action nobody looked at, and a relying party cannot tell “the policy refused this” from “the policy never saw it.”

2 · Why this belongs in guidance, not in one implementation
Three builds arrived at it independently and without coordination: a ZK-anchored denial, an attested one, and a recompute one. A rule rediscovered three times by people not talking to each other is a property of the boundary, not of any codebase.

3 · The state space
A verdict system over an action has four states, not two. Collapsing any pair of them loses a distinction some consumer needs.

state meaning provable?
ALLOW a rule authorized this yes
DENIED a rule prohibits this yes
NOT-PERMITTED nothing authorized this — default-deny, no rule fired yes
COULD-NOT-EVALUATE the engine was unreachable, the verdict expired, the domain is unregistered no — see §5
The middle two are the ones implementations conflate, because both are decision = 0. They are different claims. A consumer gating an irreversible action has to tell them apart: a rule prohibits this is a policy statement about the action; nothing authorized this is a statement about the policy’s coverage. The second can be a gap in the allowlist rather than a judgment about the act.

4 · The distinction MUST be carried, not inferred
A conforming verdict MUST carry its kind as a committed value, on every surface a consumer reads.

Three placements are possible and only one works:

Root semantics — “this root is a denylist” — is the trusted-label problem. A bytes32 root is opaque, so the claim lives in off-chain convention a reader must take on faith. It cannot be the carrier.
Domain separation alone cannot carry it either: kind is a property of the individual verdict, not only of the domain. A domain MAY declare which kinds it accepts — that narrows the field, it does not replace it.
A committed public input makes the kind part of what the proof attests. It is bound into the proof so it cannot be relabeled, and it is self-describing to the verifier and the consumer.
And “the consumer” means the on-chain consumer. A kind proven in-circuit but absent from the consumed verdict struct and from the anchor’s read surface is not carried — it is carried up to the boundary and dropped there. Conformance requires the kind to survive to the last surface a relying party actually reads.

Consequence, and it is the right one: public inputs stop being byte-identical across ALLOW and the two DENY forms. They are different claims and the encoding should say so.

5 · COULD-NOT-EVALUATE must not be provable
A system MUST NOT be able to produce a decision = 0 proof for an action it did not evaluate.

Could-not-evaluate is a liveness failure, never a verdict. It produces no proof, or a revert — never a denial. The moment an unreachable engine can emit something a Guard consumes as DENY, the gate’s silence and the gate’s judgment become the same artifact, and non-suppression is lost from the other end.

This is the mirror of §1: §1 says a denial must leave a trace; §5 says an absence must not manufacture one.

6 · Conformance is a negative vector, not a paragraph
An implementation claiming this section should show, for each state, an input it refuses and a test that fails when the refusal is removed:

a DENY that leaves no readable trace → rejected
a NOT-PERMITTED indistinguishable from a DENIED → rejected
an unevaluated action that yields a decision = 0 proof → rejected
a kind present in-circuit but absent from the consumed verdict → rejected
The two states that are trivially confused are exactly the two that go unchecked by default.

On your question of §4 or §6: I put the state space at §3 and the carriage requirement at §4, because the fourth state and policy_kind are the same idea — a taxonomy is only real if the distinctions are carried. Splitting them would let someone adopt the words and drop the mechanism. Reorder freely.

The three-role split is right, and it fixes something I raised badly. My version said “pay correct dissent” and stopped there — yours separates who noticed from who escalated, which are different acts with different risk, and pays them differently. That’s the part I missed.

It also quietly solves the checkpoint problem I raised at point 4. Three things I’d want pinned before this is built.

1 · What happens when dissent is wrong is unspecified — and it decides everything
The mechanism describes payouts when dissent is vindicated: first dissenter takes the opposing side’s slashed stake, follow-ups get their stake back.

It doesn’t say what a dissenter loses when the majority turns out to be right.

If the answer is “nothing — they get their stake back,” then dissenting first on every checkpoint is a dominant strategy: free when wrong, paid when right. That floods the record with dissent, destroys the signal value of dissent, and the honest participant who dissents only when they actually spot something is indistinguishable from the lottery player.

So wrong dissent has to cost something. But note the tension with your own goal — make it cost too much and you rebuild the silence problem this refinement exists to solve. My instinct is that wrong dissent should cost less than a wrong challenge and more than nothing, which fits the three-tier risk ladder you’ve already built. Worth stating explicitly rather than leaving to implementation.

2 · “First” needs an ordering authority, and this makes ordering worth buying
First-dissenter takes the whole opposing stake; follow-up dissenters get nothing. So the difference between first and second is the entire payout, decided by ordering.

That makes transaction ordering economically valuable at exactly the checkpoint where honesty is being measured. Whoever controls sequencing — a sequencer, a relay, a mempool position — can convert that control into the first-dissenter reward, or sell it. And the system’s whole premise is that we don’t trust ordering.

Options, none free: order by a commitment (dissenters commit-then-reveal, so position is fixed before content is visible), split the first-dissenter reward across everyone who dissented within a window, or accept ordering as a trusted input and say so plainly. The last is a legitimate choice — but it’s a trust assumption and should be written down as one rather than inherited from the chain by default.

3 · The global pool is thinnest exactly when a challenge matters most
The challenger’s reward should be “significantly larger than the total voting stake of this checkpoint.” That’s the right target. The pool that funds it is filled by past slashes.

So: a healthy system produces few slashes, which means a small pool, which means the guarantee can’t be met — and challenging is least rewarded precisely when violations are rarest, which is when catching one is most valuable. A system that has been honest for a year is the one where challenging pays worst.

That’s not a flaw in the design, it’s a solvency constraint the design needs an answer to: a floor funded from something other than slashes (protocol fee, requester escrow), or an explicit statement that challenge rewards degrade as the pool empties so nobody plans around a guarantee that isn’t there.

We spent a day and a half going through the org’s repos properly rather than reactively. Worth writing down what it found, because the pattern matters more than the individual fixes — and it implicates us as much as anyone.

The headline
Almost nothing was found by reading. Nearly everything was found by running.

a stale README asserting a Solidity interface didn’t exist, when three did — survived until an outsider opened the file
a Go test returning ok (cached) on a changed vector file — a false green, caught only by tampering with a vector on purpose
“golden vector readers” that might have been inline copies — proved real by corrupting a vector and watching all four languages fail
three Rust address-parsing bugs, including one file using two different separators
a nonce race presenting as three failing tests, which was never a code bug at all
a WaitMined race in a Go client, and then three more instances of it that pass today only on timing luck
a suppression vector in a live ledger where one unanchored citation could permanently null a settled reading — and after the first fix, the same vector still worked through a second door
a CORS requirement nobody had written down, where an endpoint is unreachable while being perfectly healthy and curl returns 200
a Docker publish broken since 22 June — six weeks, ~18 unread notifications, on an account nobody checks
an edge rule whose central predicate (“distinct lanes”) was never defined and never checked
Every one of those was in a system whose authors — us included — believed it was fine.

The thing I’d actually propose
Don’t close an issue on the strength of a description. Close it on the strength of something that fails when you break it.

Concretely, three habits that caught most of the above:

Run the thing, don’t read the thing. Every finding above came from executing something. Several times the code looked right and was wrong.
Break it on purpose and check you notice. Tamper with a vector, sign with the wrong key, delete the qualifier, drop a signature. If nothing fails, the check isn’t a check. kenneives’ independence rubric in giskard’s repo is the clearest example of this done well — a negative fixture whose failing is the proof the rubric works.
Fix the class, not the instance. This is the one we got wrong most. A current field was fixed and the vector survived through disputed. A hardcoded version was fixed in one file and the same bug sat one file over. A WaitMined was added to one client while three others still lack it. Every time, the instance fix was correct and insufficient.
Our own mistakes, since a list of other people’s would be worthless
merged a PR unreviewed inside another PR, by branching without returning to main — after saying explicitly it should wait for review
posted “clear to merge” ten minutes after an amendment we hadn’t read
proposed a three-line fix that addressed the reported instance and left the class open
diagnosed a whole class of test failures as “needs an RPC” and repeated it in a merge message; it was a missing sibling checkout
reported someone’s new test as failing when our own simulation had broken it
nearly required a CI check on a repo where no workflow runs on PRs, which would have blocked every future PR permanently
What changed structurally
Two repos had no CI at all and now have it. The object that crosses the cutoff boundary should probably be an admission receipt, not just a DA artifact with a timestamp. Minimal shape:
contribution_admission.v0
  artifact_cid
  accepted_at
  acceptance_seq
  epoch_id
  acceptance_policy_commitment
  agent_id
  signature_or_attestation
accepted_at answers when the contribution became admitted; acceptance_seq gives deterministic ordering and removes clock-tie ambiguity; acceptance_policy_commitment binds the exact admission policy in force at that moment. Then the daily membership predicate can be stated independently of DA replication or chain latency:
A contribution belongs to epoch e iff a valid admission receipt for its artifact was issued under the policy committed for e, with accepted_at < cutoff(e). Subsequent DA replication, anchor confirmation, retry, or acknowledgement MUST NOT change epoch membership.
The frozen enumerable set is therefore the ordered set of valid admission receipts satisfying that predicate. contributionRoot commits to those receipts (or their canonical hashes), not merely to whatever anchor transactions happened to have confirmed by cutoff.
That gives three separate states which should not collapse into one another:
admitted — historical membership in the work set;
anchored — publication / settlement state;
verified — judgment or proof state.
An anchor can still lag the cutoff, but it cannot move a contribution into the wrong day. Likewise, a later policy edit cannot reinterpret an already-admitted contribution.
I think this fits the thin-Substrate boundary well: the Substrate does not decide contribution value, but it does need to produce a tamper-evident fact about what entered the enumerable set, under which policy, and when.
Fede’s /review precedent seems like the right implementation model here; this just makes the cutoff primitive explicit enough that the later TEE/ZK assurance phases do not inherit an ambiguous admission boundary.

acceptance_seq is the right primitive -- we hit the identical need and solved it with a locked reserve_entry_number() (services/ledger_chain.py): every ledger writer takes a file lock, reads the current max entry number, returns max+1, releases. Two short lock windows instead of one long one, so it doesn't force writers into a single serialized loop, and it's shared across every writer script, not per-process state. Same guarantee you want: two admissions racing the same instant still get a strict total order.

acceptance_seq                → relative position
prev_receipt_hash             → one history, not two
acceptance_policy_commitment  → which rules applied

All four make the Assist Agent’s chain self-consistent. None of them binds that

1 · Continuity stops equivocation. It does not stop backdating.

prev_receipt_hash means an agent cannot maintain two histories. It does not

verifies. acceptance_seq is monotone. The chain is honest about its shape and

agent controls.

This is not a corner case for TAS specifically: anchoring is designed to lag the

The fix is small and reuses what is already there: the freeze must commit to a

epoch_freeze.v0
  epoch_id
  cutoff
  head_at_cutoff        # admission-chain head observed AT the cutoff
  head_published_ref    # where that head was visible before the cutoff
                        # (anchor tx, relay event, DA object — any of them)

Membership becomes “a valid admission receipt in the chain that terminates at
head_at_cutoff”, not “a receipt whose accepted_at is small enough”. The
agent’s clock stops being load-bearing on its own; it only has to agree with a

legibility — it just stops being the sole authority for which day you get paid.

Excluded on purpose, since you asked specifically what and why:
- accepted_at -- this is the one that matters most for your question. It's a SIBLING field on the receipt (used to compute response_deadline), never folded into the commitment itself. If it were included, the commitment would be unique per-admission instead of shared across every admission made under the same policy table -- which breaks the actual point: two receipts issued minutes apart under the same policy_version/request_class should produce the IDENTICAL commitment, so an auditor can group receipts by 'which rule applied' without trusting any of them individually. Folding in a runtime timestamp turns a rule-identity hash into an instance hash.
- requester_identity, artifact_hash -- both live on the receipt, neither affects which policy table was in force, so neither belongs in a commitment that's supposed to answer 'which rules applied,' not 'to whom' or 'about what.'
- admission_index, response_deadline -- both DERIVED from the commitment's own inputs (delta_seconds is literally one of the three fields), so including them would make the commitment partially circular -- computed from something it also claims to authenticate.

Net effect: the commitment answers exactly one question (which table, verbatim) and nothing else leaks in. That symmetry is probably the right bar for acceptance_policy_commitment too -- whatever's in it should be the stuff that changes ONLY when the rules change, not when an individual admission happens.

I think the remaining two pieces can be made explicit without adding more authority to accepted_at.
1. Ternary epoch-membership predicate
For contribution a and epoch e:
included iff there exists exactly one valid admission receipt for a, its policy commitment is recognized for e, its chain position is continuous with the published admission history, and accepted_at < cutoff(e).
excluded iff a unique valid receipt is established and it deterministically falls outside e — e.g. accepted_at >= cutoff(e) or it is bound to another epoch.
unresolved iff membership cannot be established uniquely: missing receipt, unverifiable signature/attestation, forked sequence/history, unavailable predecessor, or conflicting valid-looking receipts.
Only included enters the frozen enumerable set. unresolved must fail closed rather than silently becoming excluded, because “we cannot establish admission history” is different from “this artifact was definitely not admitted for this epoch.”
2. Anti-backdating rule
accepted_at is an admission-time fact, but it must not carry authority by itself. Its authority comes from the receipt’s position in the append-only admission history:
acceptance_seq + prev_receipt_hash + published/broadcast chain head.
A receipt claiming accepted_at < cutoff(e) is not sufficient for inclusion if it first appears only in a chain continuation published after the cutoff with no pre-cutoff commitment covering that position.
So the stronger rule is:
Epoch membership is determined from the earliest non-equivocating admission-history commitment that covers the receipt, not from the timestamp field alone.
That prevents an Assist Agent from inserting a post-cutoff receipt later with a backdated accepted_at, while still allowing DA or on-chain anchoring itself to lag.
This keeps the surfaces separate:
acceptance_policy_commitment → which rule applied
accepted_at → claimed admission time
acceptance_seq → total order
prev_receipt_hash → continuity
published chain head → anti-equivocation / anti-backdating evidence
epoch predicate → included / excluded / unresolved
Later anchoring and verdicts only cite this admission history; neither is allowed to rewrite membership.
